claim: The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) is a member of the ENaC/DEG superfamily.
source: The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), a member of the ENaC/DEG superfamily, regulates Na+ and water homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a classification of ENaC within a known protein superfamily.

claim: ENaC regulates Na+ and water homeostasis.
source: The epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), a member of the ENaC/DEG superfamily, regulates Na+ and water homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a functional role of ENaC.

claim: ENaCs assemble as heterotrimeric channels.
source: ENaCs assemble as heterotrimeric channels that harbor protease-sensitive domains critical for gating the channel.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the assembly of ENaC.

claim: ENaCs harbor protease-sensitive domains critical for gating the channel.
source: ENaCs assemble as heterotrimeric channels that harbor protease-sensitive domains critical for gating the channel.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing a functional feature of ENaC.

claim: The structure of human ENaC in the uncleaved state was determined by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Here, we present the structure of human ENaC in the uncleaved state determined by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as the main finding of the study.

claim: The ion channel is composed of a large extracellular domain and a narrow transmembrane domain.
source: The ion channel is composed of a large extracellular domain and a narrow transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the structural composition of ENaC.

claim: ENaC assembles with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry of α:β:γ subunits.
source: The structure reveals that ENaC assembles with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry of α:β:γ subunits arranged in a counter-clockwise manner.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding from the structure.

claim: The α:β:γ subunits are arranged in a counter-clockwise manner.
source: The structure reveals that ENaC assembles with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry of α:β:γ subunits arranged in a counter-clockwise manner.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a finding from the structure.

claim: The shape of each ENaC subunit is reminiscent of a hand with key gating domains of a 'finger' and a 'thumb.'
source: The shape of each subunit is reminiscent of a hand with key gating domains of a 'finger' and a 'thumb.'
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the structural features of ENaC subunits.

claim: The protease-sensitive inhibitory domain is wedged between the finger and thumb domains.
source: Wedged between these domains is the elusive protease-sensitive inhibitory domain poised to regulate conformational changes of the 'finger' and 'thumb'; thus, the structure provides the first view of the architecture of inhibition of ENaC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the location of the inhibitory domain.

claim: The protease-sensitive inhibitory domain is poised to regulate conformational changes of the finger and thumb domains.
source: Wedged between these domains is the elusive protease-sensitive inhibitory domain poised to regulate conformational changes of the 'finger' and 'thumb'; thus, the structure provides the first view of the architecture of inhibition of ENaC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The structure provides the first view of the architecture of inhibition of ENaC.
source: Wedged between these domains is the elusive protease-sensitive inhibitory domain poised to regulate conformational changes of the 'finger' and 'thumb'; thus, the structure provides the first view of the architecture of inhibition of ENaC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: ENaC is related in amino acid sequence to acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) found in eukaryotes.
source: The fine-tuning of Na+ homeostasis is largely mediated by epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) that are related in amino acid sequence to acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) found in eukaryotes, degenerin channels (DEG) of Caenorhabditis elegans, and the FMRF-amide peptide-gated channels (FaNaCh) of mollusk (Driscoll and Chalfie, 1991; Chalfie and Wolinsky, 1990; Kellenberger and Schild, 2002; Waldmann et al., 1997a; Waldmann et al., 1997b; Krishtal and Pidoplichko, 1981; Chelur et al., 2002; Garty and Palmer, 1997; Cottrell et al., 1990; Lingueglia et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaC is related in amino acid sequence to degenerin channels (DEG) of Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: The fine-tuning of Na+ homeostasis is largely mediated by epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) that are related in amino acid sequence to acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) found in eukaryotes, degenerin channels (DEG) of Caenorhabditis elegans, and the FMRF-amide peptide-gated channels (FaNaCh) of mollusk (Driscoll and Chalfie, 1991; Chalfie and Wolinsky, 1990; Kellenberger and Schild, 2002; Waldmann et al., 1997a; Waldmann et al., 1997b; Krishtal and Pidoplichko, 1981; Chelur et al., 2002; Garty and Palmer, 1997; Cottrell et al., 1990; Lingueglia et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaC is related in amino acid sequence to FMRF-amide peptide-gated channels (FaNaCh) of mollusk.
source: The fine-tuning of Na+ homeostasis is largely mediated by epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) that are related in amino acid sequence to acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) found in eukaryotes, degenerin channels (DEG) of Caenorhabditis elegans, and the FMRF-amide peptide-gated channels (FaNaCh) of mollusk (Driscoll and Chalfie, 1991; Chalfie and Wolinsky, 1990; Kellenberger and Schild, 2002; Waldmann et al., 1997a; Waldmann et al., 1997b; Krishtal and Pidoplichko, 1981; Chelur et al., 2002; Garty and Palmer, 1997; Cottrell et al., 1990; Lingueglia et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaC/DEG ion channels are voltage-independent.
source: These ion channels belong to the voltage-independent, Na+-selective, and amiloride-sensitive ENaC/DEG superfamily which together perform diverse cellular functions in different organisms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a characteristic of the ENaC/DEG superfamily.

claim: ENaC/DEG ion channels are Na+-selective.
source: These ion channels belong to the voltage-independent, Na+-selective, and amiloride-sensitive ENaC/DEG superfamily which together perform diverse cellular functions in different organisms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a characteristic of the ENaC/DEG superfamily.

claim: ENaC/DEG ion channels are amiloride-sensitive.
source: These ion channels belong to the voltage-independent, Na+-selective, and amiloride-sensitive ENaC/DEG superfamily which together perform diverse cellular functions in different organisms.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction as a characteristic of the ENaC/DEG superfamily.

claim: ENaCs are expressed at the apical surface of epithelial tissues throughout the body.
source: In humans, ENaCs are expressed at the apical surface of epithelial tissues throughout the body, and play critical roles that range from regulation of total-body salt, water, and blood volume, to modulating airway surface liquid clearance in epithelial cells in the lungs (Büsst, 2013; Ismailov et al., 1996; Rossier et al., 2015; McDonald et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaCs play critical roles in regulation of total-body salt, water, and blood volume.
source: In humans, ENaCs are expressed at the apical surface of epithelial tissues throughout the body, and play critical roles that range from regulation of total-body salt, water, and blood volume, to modulating airway surface liquid clearance in epithelial cells in the lungs (Büsst, 2013; Ismailov et al., 1996; Rossier et al., 2015; McDonald et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaCs modulate airway surface liquid clearance in epithelial cells in the lungs.
source: In humans, ENaCs are expressed at the apical surface of epithelial tissues throughout the body, and play critical roles that range from regulation of total-body salt, water, and blood volume, to modulating airway surface liquid clearance in epithelial cells in the lungs (Büsst, 2013; Ismailov et al., 1996; Rossier et al., 2015; McDonald et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in ENaC cause severe hypertension, as in Liddle syndrome.
source: The importance of ENaC in Na+ homeostasis is highlighted by gain-of-function mutations causing severe hypertension, as in Liddle syndrome, or loss-of-function mutations causing the neonatal salt-wasting disorder pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA-1) (Gründer et al., 1997; Hansson et al., 1995; Shimkets et al., 1994; Chang et al., 1996; Edelheit et al., 2005; Kerem et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ENaC cause the neonatal salt-wasting disorder pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA-1).
source: The importance of ENaC in Na+ homeostasis is highlighted by gain-of-function mutations causing severe hypertension, as in Liddle syndrome, or loss-of-function mutations causing the neonatal salt-wasting disorder pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA-1) (Gründer et al., 1997; Hansson et al., 1995; Shimkets et al., 1994; Chang et al., 1996; Edelheit et al., 2005; Kerem et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaC dysfunction contributes to essential hypertension, heart failure, and nephrotic syndrome.
source: More subtle ENaC dysfunction contributes to diseases as diverse as essential hypertension, heart failure, and nephrotic syndrome (Soundararajan et al., 2010; Hamm et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ENaCs require three different subunits (α, β, and γ) to form a functional channel.
source: ENaCs require three different subunits to form a functional channel, α, β, and γ (Canessa et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The number of subunits in an active ENaC channel remains unclear despite decades of study.
source: Despite decades of study, the number of subunits in an active channel remains unclear (Shobair et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: ENaCs are activated by proteolysis of peptidyl tracts embedded in the extracellular domain.
source: Unique among the ENaC/DEG channels, ENaCs are activated by proteolysis of peptidyl tracts embedded in the extracellular domain (ECD), which releases inhibitory peptides.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction describing a unique feature of ENaC.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of ENaC releases inhibitory peptides.
source: Unique among the ENaC/DEG channels, ENaCs are activated by proteolysis of peptidyl tracts embedded in the extracellular domain (ECD), which releases inhibitory peptides.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction describing the mechanism of ENaC activation.

claim: The cleavage event increases channel opening probability (Po).
source: The cleavage event increases channel opening probability, Po (Orce et al., 1980; Vallet et al., 1997; Vallet et al., 2002; Vuagniaux et al., 2002; Hughey et al., 2004; Hughey et al., 2003; Caldwell et al., 2004; Passero et al., 2010; Kleyman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Only the β subunit lacks the characteristic motifs for protease recognition.
source: Amino acid sequence alignments and biochemical analyses in the ECD have so far revealed that only the β subunit lacks the characteristic motifs for protease recognition.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction based on sequence analysis.

claim: ENaCs are substrates of serine proteases like furin.
source: ENaCs are widely known as substrates of serine proteases like furin, and a growing list of proteases that recognize sites in ENaC suggests a multifaceted regulation of channel function (Rossier and Stutts, 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Full-length ENaC showed a low, wide peak in FSEC, indicating a poorly expressing polydisperse population unsuitable for cryo-EM.
source: We found a low, wide peak, indicating a poorly expressing polydisperse population unsuitable for cryo-EM (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by Figure 1a showing the FSEC trace.

claim: ΔENaC was designed by screening deletions and mutations in each ENaC subunit.
source: We thus screened a number of deletions and mutations in each ENaC subunit, harnessing information derived from previous biochemical and functional experiments gauging the propensity for heterotrimeric formation of ENaC and its susceptibility to proteolytic processing (Canessa et al., 1994; Orce et al., 1980; Vallet et al., 1997; Vallet et al., 2002; Vuagniaux et al., 2002; Hughey et al., 2004; Hughey et al., 2003; Caldwell et al., 2004; Passero et al., 2010), before arriving at the construct referred to here as ΔENaC (Figure 1a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations and figures.

claim: ΔENaC is composed of αβγ subunits truncated at the N- and C-termini.
source: ΔENaC is composed of αβγ subunits truncated at the N- and C-termini (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The Δα and Δγ subunits possess mutations in the identified furin and prostasin sites which prevent subunit cleavage and channel activation.
source: Additionally, the Δα and Δγ subunits possess mutations in the identified furin and prostasin sites which prevent subunit cleavage and channel activation (Hughey et al., 2003; Bruns et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: Neither Δα nor Δβ were modified with affinity tags because there is strong evidence that the α subunit can readily form functional homomeric channels.
source: For protein purification, neither Δα nor Δβ were modified with affinity tags because there is strong evidence that the α subunit can readily form functional homomeric channels, and the termini of Δβ are sensitive to perturbations (Canessa et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The termini of Δβ are sensitive to perturbations.
source: For protein purification, neither Δα nor Δβ were modified with affinity tags because there is strong evidence that the α subunit can readily form functional homomeric channels, and the termini of Δβ are sensitive to perturbations (Canessa et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Δγ contains both GFP and a Strep-II tag at the N-terminus.
source: As a result, Δγ contains both GFP and a Strep-II tag at the N-terminus (Figure 1c), minimizing contamination by homomeric Δα channels during purification.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The inherent pseudosymmetry from common secondary and tertiary structures between the α, β, and γ subunits of human ENaC hindered particle alignment.
source: However, the inherent pseudosymmetry from common secondary and tertiary structures between the α, β, and γ subunits of human ENaC hindered particle alignment (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Two fragment-antigen binding domains (Fabs) were isolated that recognize different epitopes (7B1 and 10D4).
source: Two fragment-antigen binding domains (Fabs) were isolated that recognize different epitopes (7B1 and 10D4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the generation of antibodies.

claim: Both Fabs 7B1 and 10D4 bind to both ΔENaC expressed in HEK 293S GnTI- and FL-ENaC expressed in HEK293T/17.
source: While these antibodies were raised against ΔENaCASIC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b), both Fabs bind to both ΔENaC expressed in HEK 293S GnTI- and FL-ENaC expressed in HEK293T/17, which indicates that ΔENaC is properly folded and that the Fabs do not bind to the ASIC segment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: The binding of both Fabs to ΔENaC and FL-ENaC indicates that ΔENaC is properly folded.
source: While these antibodies were raised against ΔENaCASIC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b), both Fabs bind to both ΔENaC expressed in HEK 293S GnTI- and FL-ENaC expressed in HEK293T/17, which indicates that ΔENaC is properly folded and that the Fabs do not bind to the ASIC segment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from the binding data.

claim: The Fabs do not bind to the ASIC segment.
source: While these antibodies were raised against ΔENaCASIC (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b), both Fabs bind to both ΔENaC expressed in HEK 293S GnTI- and FL-ENaC expressed in HEK293T/17, which indicates that ΔENaC is properly folded and that the Fabs do not bind to the ASIC segment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c,d; Figure 1—figure supplement 4a,b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from the binding data.

claim: Inclusion of 7B1 and 10D4 allowed for proper alignment of the particles.
source: Inclusion of 7B1 and 10D4 allowed for proper alignment of the particles (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Each Fab recognizes only one subunit.
source: Moreover, maps of the particles with only 10D4 (monoFab) compared to those with both 10D4 and 7B1 (diFab) show that each Fab recognizes only one subunit (Figure 1—figure supplement 4c–f).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: ΔENaC does not exhibit amiloride-sensitive currents in oocytes and HEK cells.
source: Unlike FL-ENaC (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), ΔENaC does not exhibit amiloride-sensitive currents in oocytes and HEK cells, and the only Na+-specific currents resemble those from uninjected oocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures showing electrophysiology data.

claim: Oocytes expressing ENaC channels with restored protease sites in the Δ subunits (Δα* and Δγ*) to form Δ*ENaC did not present amiloride-sensitive currents.
source: Similarly, oocytes expressing ENaC channels with restored protease sites in the Δ subunits (Δα* and Δγ*) to form Δ*ENaC did not present amiloride-sensitive currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by figures showing electrophysiology data.

claim: ΔENaC is not trafficked to the plasma membrane.
source: Based on the confocal imaging results, ΔENaC is not trafficked to the plasma membrane, in agreement with the electrophysiology results in HEK 293S GnTI- cells and oocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: Channels comprising Δα-FLβ-FLγ conduct amiloride-sensitive Na+ currents which increase approximately 5-fold upon trypsin treatment.
source: Channels comprising Δα-FLβ-FLγ conduct amiloride-sensitive Na+ currents which increase approximately 5-fold upon trypsin treatment (compared with 2.2-fold for FL-ENaC, Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data in figures.

claim: Δα adopts a biologically relevant fold, capable of forming active channels with other full-length subunits.
source: These results, in addition to the cleavage pattern of an anti-α immunoblot (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) indicate that Δα adopts a biologically relevant fold, capable of forming active channels with other full-length subunits, and that it is likely cleaved once at its N-terminal furin site (RSRA in Δα) but not the C-terminal furin site (AAAA in Δα, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from electrophysiology and immunoblot data.

claim: Δα is likely cleaved once at its N-terminal furin site (RSRA in Δα) but not the C-terminal furin site (AAAA in Δα).
source: These results, in addition to the cleavage pattern of an anti-α immunoblot (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) indicate that Δα adopts a biologically relevant fold, capable of forming active channels with other full-length subunits, and that it is likely cleaved once at its N-terminal furin site (RSRA in Δα) but not the C-terminal furin site (AAAA in Δα, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section as an inference from immunoblot data.

claim: The FLα-Δβ-FLγ channels conducted amiloride-sensitive Na+ currents with a post-trypsin/pre-trypsin ratio of 1.5.
source: The FLα-Δβ-FLγ channels conducted amiloride-sensitive Na+ currents with a post-trypsin/pre-trypsin ratio of 1.5 (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 1), similar to that of FL-ENaC.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: An anti-β immunoblot shows no cleavage of Δβ, as expected.
source: Moreover, an anti-β immunoblot shows no cleavage of Δβ, as expected (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data.

claim: The FLα-FLβ-Δγ channel conduct an amiloride-sensitive Na+ current with approximately 9.5-fold increase upon trypsin treatment.
source: The FLα-FLβ-Δγ channel also conduct an amiloride-sensitive Na+ current with approximately 9.5-fold increase upon trypsin treatment (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The structure of ΔENaC diFab complex in n-Dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM) was solved by cryoEM.
source: We solved the structure of ΔENaC diFab complex in n-Dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM) by cryoEM (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: The cryo-EM potential map has a nominal resolution of 4.2 Å based on the gold standard FSC = 0.143 and solvent adjusted FSC = 0.143 criteria.
source: We first carried out cycles of 2D and 3D classifications to remove ice contamination, micelles, and denatured complexes. The remaining particles were subjected to unsupervised ab initio 3D classification and refinement in cryoSPARC (Punjani et al., 2017) as well as 3D classification and refinement in cisTEM (Grant et al., 2018) to arrive at the cryo-EM potential map with a nominal resolution of 4.2 Å from both programs, based on the gold standard FSC = 0.143 and solvent adjusted FSC = 0.143 criteria, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the resolution of the cryo-EM map.

claim: A masked refinement excluding the flexible Fc domains of the Fabs and micelle in cisTEM obtained a map at 3.9 Å.
source: Additionally, we conducted a masked refinement excluding the flexible Fc domains of the Fabs and micelle in cisTEM (Figure 3a), and obtained a map at 3.9 Å, as determined by the solvent adjusted FSC = 0.143 criterion (Figure 3b,c), with local resolution estimates generated by BSoft (Heymann and Belnap, 2007) indicating regions of the map with a resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section describing the improved resolution after masked refinement.

claim: Local resolution estimates indicate regions of the map with a resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: Additionally, we conducted a masked refinement excluding the flexible Fc domains of the Fabs and micelle in cisTEM (Figure 3a), and obtained a map at 3.9 Å, as determined by the solvent adjusted FSC = 0.143 criterion (Figure 3b,c), with local resolution estimates generated by BSoft (Heymann and Belnap, 2007) indicating regions of the map with a resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Results section and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Alignment of predicted glycosylation sites and aromatic residues to distinct features in the map allowed for the correct assignment of the homology models of the ENaC ECD.
source: Alignment of predicted glycosylation sites and aromatic residues to distinct features in the map allowed for the correct assignment of the homology models of the ENaC ECD, generated from the desensitized state of ASIC (PDB: 2QTS, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the model building process.

claim: The β subunit is predicted to have 11 glycosylation sites by primary sequence, considerably more than α or γ.
source: The β subunit is predicted to have 11 glycosylation sites by primary sequence, considerably more than α or γ.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the identification of subunits.

claim: Six prominent glycosylation sites were used to assign β (as opposed to the three each in α and γ).
source: Six prominent glycosylation sites were used to assign β (as opposed to the three each in α and γ), whereas a glycosylation on the β9-α4 loop distinguished α from γ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: A glycosylation on the β9-α4 loop distinguished α from γ.
source: Six prominent glycosylation sites were used to assign β (as opposed to the three each in α and γ), whereas a glycosylation on the β9-α4 loop distinguished α from γ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: 7B1 binds the α subunit.
source: Guided by these features and the 10D4 monoFab ΔENaC map, we assigned the identity of 7B1 and 10D4 as binding α and β subunits, respectively (Figure 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: 10D4 binds the β subunit.
source: Guided by these features and the 10D4 monoFab ΔENaC map, we assigned the identity of 7B1 and 10D4 as binding α and β subunits, respectively (Figure 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: Forming a trimeric ensemble, the α-β-γ subunits arrange in a counterclockwise manner.
source: Forming a trimeric ensemble, the α-β-γ subunits arrange in a counterclockwise manner, as reported by previous studies (Collier and Snyder, 2011; Collier et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 4b,d).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with supporting citations and figures.

claim: The overall domain organization within each subunit of ΔENaC concurs with that of ASIC.
source: The overall domain organization within each subunit of ΔENaC concurs with that of ASIC, which was first illustrated in the crystal structure of chicken ASIC (cASIC) (Jasti et al., 2007) (chicken ASIC shares 18 – 20% sequence identity with human ENaC; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a supporting citation and figures.

claim: Chicken ASIC shares 18 – 20% sequence identity with human ENaC.
source: The overall domain organization within each subunit of ΔENaC concurs with that of ASIC, which was first illustrated in the crystal structure of chicken ASIC (cASIC) (Jasti et al., 2007) (chicken ASIC shares 18 – 20% sequence identity with human ENaC; Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section.

claim: Each subunit of ΔENaC harbors a cysteine-rich ECD resembling a hand with the palm, knuckle, finger, and thumb domains clenching a 'ball' of β strands.
source: Each subunit of ΔENaC harbors a cysteine-rich ECD resembling a hand with the palm, knuckle, finger, and thumb domains clenching a 'ball' of β strands.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the structural features.

claim: This compact organization is stabilized by eight disulfide bridges in the ECDs of α and γ and nine in β.
source: This compact organization is stabilized by eight disulfide bridges in the ECDs of α and γ and nine in β.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the structural features.

claim: Seven of the disulfide bonds are conserved throughout the ENaC/DEG family.
source: Seven of the disulfide bonds are conserved throughout the ENaC/DEG family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 5a–c).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: The eighth disulfide bond is unique to the three ENaC subunits.
source: The eighth is unique to the three ENaC subunits.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the disulfide bonds.

claim: ENaC differs significantly from ASIC in both structure and primary sequence at the knuckle and finger domains.
source: ENaC differs significantly from ASIC in both structure and primary sequence at the knuckle and finger domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: Each knuckle domain in ENaC makes extensive interactions with the α1 and α2 helices of the finger domain in the adjacent subunit.
source: Each knuckle domain in ENaC makes extensive interactions with the α1 and α2 helices of the finger domain in the adjacent subunit (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The knuckle and finger domains of all three subunits form a 'collar' at the top of the ECD.
source: Together, the knuckle and finger domains of all three subunits form a 'collar' at the top of the ECD.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the structural features.

claim: The contact between the finger and thumb domains is mediated by long antiparallel helices α1 and α2.
source: The contact between the finger and thumb domains is mediated by long antiparallel helices α1 and α2, which form a barrier between the thumb domain and the β6-β7 loop with α2 making the primary contacts with the thumb domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: α2 makes the primary contacts with the thumb domain.
source: The contact between the finger and thumb domains is mediated by long antiparallel helices α1 and α2, which form a barrier between the thumb domain and the β6-β7 loop with α2 making the primary contacts with the thumb domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section and supported by figures.

claim: The α2 helix makes an almost 90° turn towards the palm domain breaking the helix.
source: The α2 helix makes an almost 90° turn towards the palm domain breaking the helix.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the structural features.

claim: The TMD is not well ordered, hampering the ability to model the entire TMD region and assign a functional state of the channel.
source: The TMD is not well ordered, hampering our ability to model the entire TMD region and assign a functional state of the channel.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing limitations of the structure.

claim: The overall configuration of the TMD shows that TM2 of all three subunits are positioned near the central axis, poised to mediate ion conduction.
source: The overall configuration of the TMD shows that TM2 of all three subunits are positioned near the central axis, poised to mediate ion conduction in agreement with the crystal structures of ASIC and previous elegant functional studies probing ion selectivity and channel block (Kellenberger and Schild, 2002).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The γ subunit lacks two residues preceding the palm domain.

claim: Interactions within the wrist region in the γ subunit may differ from that of α and β subunits.

claim: Stretches of 20 – 40 amino acids are pieces of larger domains located in the periphery of the ECD near subunit interfaces.

claim: These stretches of amino acids, located between α1 and α2, are unique to ENaC and are responsible for channel Gating Relief of Inhibition by Proteolysis.
source: These stretches of amino acids, located between α1 and α2 are unique to ENaC and are responsible for channel Gating Relief of Inhibition by Proteolysis and will hereafter be referred to as the GRIP domain.

claim: Each GRIP domain is composed of a core of β strands that forge interactions with the finger and thumb domains forming a β-sheet 'blanket' that conceals the α2 helix of the finger.

claim: Although the β subunit is not known to gate the channel via proteolysis, it also possesses a GRIP domain with similar organization to those of the α and γ subunits.
source: Surprisingly, although the β subunit is not known to gate the channel via proteolysis, it also possesses a GRIP domain with similar organization to those of the α and γ subunits.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as a surprising finding.

claim: In all three subunits, the GRIP domains comprise two antiparallel β strands stapled together by a disulfide bond located in the loop that rests against the thumb domain.
source: In all three subunits, the GRIP domains comprise two antiparallel β strands stapled together by a disulfide bond located in the loop that rests against the thumb domain (Figure 7b–d, Figure 7—figure supplement 1b–d).

claim: The additional disulfide bond contributes to the well-ordered behavior of the β GRIP domain.

claim: The inhibitory tracts contain the P1 strand.

claim: The first furin site lies at the N-terminal side of P1.
source: Based on this configuration, the first furin site lies at the N-terminal side of P1 whereas the second protease site (furin for α and other protease sites for γ) is likely located at the C-terminal side of P2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as an inference from the structure.

claim: The second protease site (furin for α and other protease sites for γ) is likely located at the C-terminal side of P2.
source: Based on this configuration, the first furin site lies at the N-terminal side of P1 whereas the second protease site (furin for α and other protease sites for γ) is likely located at the C-terminal side of P2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section as an inference from the structure.

claim: The anti-parallel organization of P1 and P2 strands places the two protease sites in close proximity to each other.
source: The anti-parallel organization of P1 and P2 strands places the two protease sites in close proximity to each other.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section describing the structural arrangement.

claim: The pocket that is largely occupied by α2 in ΔENaC is referred to as the aromatic pocket.

source: Tucked in the aromatic pocket, α2 makes contacts with all critical elements of the gating machinery in ENaC.

source: This observation is consistent with studies finding that site-directed mutagenesis perturbing residues in the α2 results in changes in Na+ self-inhibition and binding of the P1 segment of the GRIP domain (Kashlan et al., 2010).

claim: In all three ENaC subunits, the α2 forms contacts with the thumb, α1 helix, the β6-β7 loop and the GRIP domain, and with the knuckle and the upper palm domains in the adjacent subunit.
source: In all three ENaC subunits, the α2 forms contacts with the thumb, α1 helix, the β6-β7 loop and the GRIP domain, and with the knuckle and the upper palm domains in the adjacent subunit (Figure 8).

claim: Studies using synthesized 8-mer (LPHPLQRL) and 11-mer peptides (RFLNLIPLLVF) have identified residues in α2 to be critical to the binding of the inhibitory peptides.

source: These inhibitory peptides contain prolines that introduce a kink within the tract that may serve as a point that divides P1 into two segments: the N-terminal side, which interacts with the finger and thumb; and the C-terminal side, which interacts primarily with α2 and P3.

claim: The observed orientation of the P1 segment is consistent with cross-linking experiments showing that the inhibitory tracts adopt an extended conformation.
source: The observed orientation of the P1 segment is consistent with the cross-linking experiments by Kashlan et al., which provided two major findings: (1) the inhibitory tracts adopt an extended conformation and ﻿(2) the N-terminal side of the peptide binds near the thumb/finger interface (Kashlan et al., 2010; Kashlan et al., 2012).

claim: The N-terminal side of the peptide binds near the thumb/finger interface.
source: The observed orientation of the P1 segment is consistent with the cross-linking experiments by Kashlan et al., which provided two major findings: (1) the inhibitory tracts adopt an extended conformation and ﻿(2) the N-terminal side of the peptide binds near the thumb/finger interface (Kashlan et al., 2010; Kashlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Removal of the inhibitory tract in α transitions the channel to an intermediate Po state.
source: While removal of the inhibitory tract in α transitions the channel to an intermediate Po state, excision of the γ-P1 segment places the channel in the high Po state; this high Po state can be accomplished without the removal of the α-P1 (Carattino et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: Excision of the γ-P1 segment places the channel in the high Po state.
source: While removal of the inhibitory tract in α transitions the channel to an intermediate Po state, excision of the γ-P1 segment places the channel in the high Po state; this high Po state can be accomplished without the removal of the α-P1 (Carattino et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: The high Po state can be accomplished without the removal of the α-P1.

claim: Alterations of a conserved cysteine, α-Cys479 to an Arg, causes Liddle syndrome due to a missense mutation.
source: Underscoring the importance of the wrist region and the critical roles that disulfide bridges play in maintaining the structural and functional integrity of ENaC, alterations of a conserved cysteine, α-Cys479 to an Arg, causes Liddle syndrome due to a missense mutation that not only eliminates a disulfide bridge located at the juncture of the thumb and palm domains but also introduces a bulky, positively charged residue (Salih et al., 2017) (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Discussion section with a supporting citation and figure.
